children: By Staff Writer
A severe milk shortage in Kenya and Rwanda has prompted policymakers to blame adverse weather and declining returns from dairy farming, even as Tanzania and Uganda enjoy strong output.

This week, the Consumer Federation of Kenya (Cofek), a lobby, warned that without urgent government intervention, the situation could worsen, painting a picture of an important produce whose value chain remains weak and polarised.“Cofek is deeply concerned by the continuing decline in formal milk intake and the resultant strain on retail prices,” said Mr Stephen Mutoro, Secretary-General of the federation.“Resultant strain on retail milk prices is already being felt by consumers. We call on the Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock Development, the Kenya Dairy Board (KDB) and the National Treasury to take urgent measures to restore supplies and stabilise prices.”Some top supermarkets in Kenya have started restricting purchases to fewer than five packets while others have no milk.
Popular brands like Brookside, New KCC, Tuzo and Mt Kenya have disappeared from supermarket shelves as KDB confirmed a 3.7 percent drop in formal milk deliveries to processors.

The board, nonetheless, said it is banking on the projected heavy rainfall to improve production.“The Kenya Dairy Board wishes to reassure the public, consumers and dairy industry stakeholders that milk continues to be available in the market, despite temporary supply constraints being experienced in some parts of the country,” said KDB Managing Director William Maritim.
Dr Maritim attributed the supply constraints to seasonal factors, particularly the prevailing dry and cold conditions in key milk-producing areas.

The condition, he said, affects pasture and fodder availability, consequently putting pressure on milk production.“Formal milk deliveries to processors declined by 3.7 percent from 84.4 million litres in June to 81.3 million litres in July. The board is compiling formal milk intake data for August,” Dr Maritim added.“Preliminary indications suggest a further decline in milk deliveries, reflecting the prevailing seasonal production conditions.”Authorities blame unfavourable weather and high production costs.

It is the same situation in Rwanda, which has experienced a long period of milk shortage due to a combination of factors, including a prolonged dry spell that has devastated many parts of the country.

Rwanda has experienced an unusual dry period with its intensity, lack of traditional relief rains and record-high temperatures that made it one of the most severe and anomalous dry spells in recent years.
Combined with global warming, Rwanda tracked temperatures during the June-August dry spell that were well above normal.
With the Eastern Province, one of the leading milk production regions, hit hard and lower-lying districts experiencing heatwaves and severe water scarcity, the shortage was inevitable.
Rwanda produces close to 2.9 million litres of milk daily, according to the Ministry of Agriculture and Animal Resources.
The country’s farmers produce more than a billion litres of milk annually.
Yearly production has increased significantly in the last two decades, from roughly 332,000 litres per day in 2005.

However, milk hubs like Nyagatare and other districts in Eastern province have seen production plunge by more than half as a result of scarcity of reliable animal feed and pasture that has been scorched.“We have not experienced this kind of dryness in a long time. The situation is so bad that we have lost many animals. Scarcity of milk is affecting many livelihoods,” Mr John Ruyange, farmer in Gatsibo district of Eastern province, told The East African.

Dairy farmers say deliveries to processing plants went down significantly, with groups supplying less than half of their usual daily targets during dry spells. The supplies dropped from 90,000 litres to 40,000 in peak shortage periods, especially from July.
Retail milk prices have skyrocketed in the last five months, with a litre in capital Kigali going for $0.94. At dairy plants, it costs $0.45, up from $0.41 five months ago.

The Rwandan government recently moved away from strict administrative price controls, allowing producers and buyers to negotiate rates directly based on real-time market conditions and production costs.
Farm gate prices for a litre were set at $0.27 as a baseline for raw milk delivered at collection centres by farmers across the country.

According to the Ministry of Trade and Industry, the stakeholder-led pricing framework was introduced in 2025, and negotiations were expected to conclude before the end of last month, enabling the revised prices to be implemented without delay.“The policy shift follows concerns from farmers that the current farm-gate price no longer reflects production costs,” said Dr Solange Uwituze, the Minister Agriculture and Animal Resources.“Farmers cited rising expenses for animal feed, veterinary medicines, water, electricity, fuel and labour, arguing that the existing pricing structure has made milk production increasingly unprofitable.”Eastern province was also hit by Rift Valley Fever mid this year, leading to the government imposing strict movement and trade of meat and milk products.
The quarantine affected mainly Kigali, which depends on dairy products from provinces. It led to scarcity of milk and meat in the capital.
The government says the outbreak has been contained but the resumed trade in meat and dairy products has been restricted to ensure traceability.

Ms Grace Bageni, a milk seller in Kabeza – a suburb in the capital city – says even after the government ending the quarantine, the milk shortage persists.“We don’t get enough milk and are forced to increase prices. Customer numbers have gone down significantly because of the higher prices. Those who used to buy two or more packets of milk have reduced to one,” she said.
Overall, the shortage of milk is also as a result of other problems in the economy.
The prices of commercial feeds and basic supplements in Kenya are high, making proper nutrition for cattle expensive and reducing milk yields.
Some dairy farmers have reportedly quit and opted for other ventures.

According to the KDB, the projected rainfall October-December rainfall should improve pasture, which will in turn lead to increased milk yields.“The October-December rainfall season is expected to support recovery in pasture and fodder availability, leading to improved milk production and supply as conditions become more favourable than today,” Dr Maritim told the news briefing in Nairobi.
Kenya’s annual milk production is 5.4 billion to 5.5 billion litres, making it the largest milk producer on the continent.
Despite a prolonged dry spell, Uganda sustained its production at 5.4 billion litres, or about 15 million litres a day.
That amount is enough for the domestic market and keep the country’s processing plants running optimally, even as farmers contend with declining fodder supplies, authorities say.
Even so, Uganda’s surplus cannot easily fill the gap in Kenya.

Milk production in Kenya and Uganda is broadly comparable, but Kenya’s much larger consumer demand means its dairy industry struggles to meet local needs, says Brookside Dairies Uganda General Manager Benson Mwangi.“It’s a question of demand and supply. In Kenya, the demand is huge unlike in Uganda where milk supply is more than enough,” Mr Mwangi says.
Uganda is constrained by restrictions on milk exports to Kenya, leaving processors with limited access to the neighbouring country’s market.

Mr Samson Mpiira, Head of the Dairy Development Department at Uganda’s Ministry of Agriculture, says trade barriers in the region are the major reason Uganda’s surplus cannot help ease shortages elsewhere in the East African Community.

Mr Mwangi says restrictions on export permits leave processors in Uganda searching for alternative regional markets that cannot match Kenya’s consumer base, while the industry becomes more frustrated by national trade policies that do not make sense in a common market.“We are in the East African Community. Surely, do I need a permit to sell milk to a neighbour?” Mr Mwangi asks.

In Kenya, only 15 to 20 percent of production goes through formal processors under the KDB watch, while 80 to 85 percent moves via informal local channels like direct farm sales and cooperative societies.
Data from the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics indicates that formal-sector milk intake decreased by five percent from 88.89 million litres in May to 84.44 million litres the following month.
According to Cofek, June’s intake was 6.4 percent lower than the 90.24 million litres recorded in June 2025, pointing to growing pressure on formal milk supplies.
Officials say animal feed and dairy meal are expensive because dry and cold weather have destroyed pasture, while prices for the raw ingredients needed to manufacture commercial feed have surged.

Important ingredients used to make animal feed, such as yellow maize, soybean meal, canola and sunflower cake, have become scarce and expensive. The cost of commercial feed has gone up by roughly 45 percent.
Many of these raw components are imported, exposing local manufacturers to high shipping and foreign exchange costs.

In 2022, a 70-kilo bag of standard dairy meal averaged $17.7 (Ksh2,300) to $19.3 (Ksh2,500). A farmer with two cows consuming supplemental meals needed $34.7 (Ksh4,500) to $46.3 (Ksh6,000) per month on concentrates.
Today, a 70-kilogramme bag of dairy meal goes for $20 (Ksh2,600) to $27 (Ksh3,500) according to data from “Farmers Trend”.
That means monthly feed for two cows cost a farmer $58 (Ksh7,500) to $77.2 (Ksh10,000) when factoring in hay or silage making, making dairy farming costly.
Because feed and fodder are expensive, smallholder farmers – who produce about 80 percent of Kenya’s milk – cannot nourish their animals properly.
Daily milk production per cow has dropped from seven to nine litres to four to five litres.

Transparent recovery strategyCofek has demanded a transparent recovery strategy, emergency fodder and feed subsidies for affected dairy counties. It also wants the ministry to explain what it is doing to reduce the cost of key feed ingredients.

Mr Mutoro urged the National Treasury to waive import duty and VAT on yellow maize, soya and other dairy-meal inputs“Given the prevailing situation, we hereby demand that the National Treasury waives import duty and VAT on yellow maize, soya and other key dairy-meal inputs with immediate effect, to lower feed costs and stem the exit of dairy farmers,” he said.
Kenya registered a milk surplus last year, a matter that is now a bone of contention as stakeholders bicker on whether any lessons were learnt on how the yield was achieved.
At the time, Kenya stopped importing milk, leading to protests by dealers in Uganda.
Uganda’s dairy industry generally remains high-yielding, with some farmers going to the extent of petitioning for steady domestic processing markets for their surplus volumes.

However, milk production in parts of Western Uganda – especially in Ntungamo district – has fallen by more than half, with daily output dropping to about 40,000 litres from as much as 90,000 during the rainy season, according to authorities.
A prolonged drought, which has depleted pasture and water sources, as well as Foot and Mouth Disease (FMD), which has affected livestock in the district is to blame, the Ministry of Agriculture says.

Uganda produces at least 5.3 billion litres of milk every year, maintaining a substantial surplus. That makes Uganda a major exporter of dairy products within the East African Community, particularly to Kenya.
However, protracted milk wars over imports from Uganda due to non-tariff barriers enacted by both governments have affected the smooth flow of dairy products across the borders.
Tanzania has avoided shortages so far, though the country faces a long-term structural gap between total domestic demand and production.
Tanzania’s domestic dairy production has grown, hitting more than 4.22 billion litres this year. Local processors continue expanding their market share.

Figures presented to Parliament in Dodoma during budget proposals by Livestock and Fisheries Minister Bashiru Ally in May show that national milk production increased by 40 percent in six years, from three billion litres in the 2019/20 financial year to 4.2 billion litres in 2025/26.
Even with the output rising, processors in Tanzania utilise only a fraction of installed capacity. Raw milk collection, productivity and farmer payment remain weak.
The country’s import policy tilted the competitive advantage in its favour, with increased import duty protecting the industry and encouraging more local production.
Observers say the regional imbalance is also shaped by changing trade and processing policies.
Uganda no longer exports raw milk, instead focusing on value-added products like pasteurised milk, milk powder and a range of other consumer dairy products.
Rwanda, Mr Mpiira says, has faced persistent shortages partly because of its demand for raw milk. Greater access to Ugandan processed dairy products could ease those shortfalls, he says.
Farmers in Uganda have also felt the effects of the dry spell, but the decline in production has been modest, says Ronald Tumukunde, the Chief Executive of the Uganda Dairy Farmers Association.
For now, Uganda has enough milk to keep its own market supplied – and potentially more than it can readily sell across the border.

title: ZAWYA: Milk shortage persists in Kenya, Rwanda
